name: Peter Berlin & Lucy Edwards

summary.text: Lucy Edwards was a vice president in the Bank of New York's Eastern European division and Peter Berlin, her husband, a Russian émigré who ran fund-transfer companies including Benex and BECS. Accounts opened in those names at a Manhattan branch of the bank in 1996 received about $7 billion from Russia over roughly three and a half years. Both were indicted in Manhattan federal court in October 1999, pleaded guilty in 2000 to money-laundering conspiracy and related charges, and were ordered to pay restitution. The Bank of New York resolved the related investigations in November 2005 with a $38 million payment.

facts.claim: An indictment unsealed in U.S. District Court in Manhattan in October 1999 charged Peter Berlin, Lucy Edwards and Aleksey Volkov in connection with the movement of Russian money through Bank of New York accounts.
facts.quote: an indictment unsealed Tuesday in U.S. District Court in Manhattan charges Peter Berlin, 44, Lucy Edwards, 41, and Aleksey Volkov, 34

facts.claim: Edwards, a former Bank of New York vice president, and Berlin, her husband, pleaded guilty in February 2000 to money-laundering conspiracy, operating an illegal money services business and establishing an unauthorized foreign bank.
facts.quote: pleaded guilty in 2000 to money laundering conspiracy, operating an illegal money services business and establishing an unauthorized foreign bank

facts.claim: Edwards cooperated with prosecutors and the FBI; she was sentenced to six months of house arrest and five years of probation, and she and Berlin were ordered to pay $685,000 in restitution.
facts.quote: Edwards and Berlin were ordered to pay $685,000 in restitution

facts.claim: According to the U.S. Attorney's Office, accounts in the names of Benex International Co., Inc. and BECS International LLC were opened in 1996 at a Manhattan retail branch of the Bank of New York by Peter Berlin with the help of his wife Lucy Edwards, then a bank vice president, and about $7 billion from Russia moved through them to transferees worldwide over roughly three and a half years.
facts.quote: Peter Berlin, a Russian émigré, opened these accounts with the help of his wife, Lucy Edwards, who was a BNY vice president

facts.claim: Berlin set up three fund-transfer companies, Benex, BECS and Lowland, while Edwards worked in the bank's Eastern European division; investigators said nearly $7 billion from Russia passed through Benex and the other companies into the bank.
facts.quote: Investigators say nearly US$7 billion from Russia passed through Benex and other fund-transfer companies set up and operated by Berlin and Edwards into BONY

facts.claim: In November 2005 the Bank of New York agreed to pay $38 million in penalties and victim compensation to resolve parallel criminal investigations by the Eastern and Southern Districts of New York, including the matter of the Berlin and Edwards accounts and the bank's Bank Secrecy Act reporting failures.
facts.quote: agreed to pay $38 million in penalties and victim compensation to resolve parallel criminal investigations by the Eastern and Southern Districts of New York

openQuestions: Site claim tested: that Berlin and Edwards 'funneled over $7 billion in looted Russian enterprise revenues, IMF stabilization loans, and state capital' with 'advance knowledge of the impending default'. The $7 billion figure and the guilty pleas are supported; the characterisation of the money as IMF loans or state reserves and the claim of advance knowledge are unsupported by the sources found, and Fortune reported that U.S. prosecutors refuted the Russian government's later claim about the bank's conduct.

The site lists both as 'Peter Berlin & Lucy Edwards (Benex Worldwide)'; the corporate name in the DOJ release is Benex International Co., Inc.; whether 'Benex Worldwide' is a separate entity is unconfirmed.
The February 2000 plea date and the sentencing details come from a Reuters-sourced regional report (The Royal Gazette); the owner may wish to confirm them against the SDNY docket.
The site places the case in the context of the 1998 default; the accounts were opened in 1996 and the DOJ release describes activity over roughly three and a half years.
